description: SoloHorizon Tech builds intuitive lunar data visualization tools to evaluate Sun and Earth visibility for space mission planning.
summary: A web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when a lander should touch down near the Moon’s south pole. For selected sites and dates, it shows when the Sun (power) and the Earth (radio link) are both above the horizon, ranks the sites, and visualizes everything on a 2D polar map, a 3D Moon and a timeline.
details:
Landers near the lunar south pole need sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth for communication, but both stay close to the horizon, so conditions change strongly with site and date. Our tool answers: where and when should a lander touch down?

Users pick up to five candidate sites (Mons Mouton (IM-2), Malapert Massif, Haworth Rim, Nobile Rim 1, Peak Near Shackleton) and a date range in 2027. A Python script computes hourly Sun and Earth altitude and azimuth for every site using Skyfield and the NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris, in the Moon-fixed frame. The web app then:

  • Marks an hour as “good” when the Sun and Earth are both above the horizon, and ranks sites by their share of good time.
  • Shows the best landing window (longest unbroken good period) and the best single moment.
  • Reports the longest darkness and longest radio blackout per site.
  • Visualizes results on a south pole map, an interactive 3D Moon with a time slider, a timeline chart and a sky dome.

Built with Python (Skyfield, NumPy) for precomputation, and JavaScript, Plotly and three.js for the web app, hosted on GitHub Pages.

Limits: a flat horizon is assumed (no terrain shadowing), and sites are region centers, not exact landing points. Next, terrain horizons and more sites and dates could be added.
